issues.subcategory: Inadequate perceptual vs. memory error dissociation
issues.description: The core logic for distinguishing perceptual from memory errors relies on illusions increasing over time. However, this logic is incomplete: if perceptual illusions occur on some proportion of trials, those trials would contribute a constant baseline of errors at all delays, while memory illusions add on top. The authors cannot rule out a mixed model where both perceptual and memory illusions co-occur. The increase over time shows memory illusions exist, but does not establish that perceptual illusions are absent or minimal. The authors acknowledge this briefly but do not quantify the potential perceptual contribution or provide a formal model comparison.
issues.quote: If the frequency of reported illusions increases over time, then at least part of the illusions can be attributed to memory processing rather than perceptual encoding. After all, at both time points initial perceptual processing was finished, so if the illusions arose completely during perception, they ought not to increase over time.

issues.subcategory: Absence of immediate (0 ms delay) baseline condition
issues.description: To properly establish that illusions increase over time, a true perceptual baseline (probe presented simultaneously with or immediately at offset of the memory display, before any memory decay) is needed. The shortest delay used is 500-750 ms, which is already well beyond iconic memory duration (<500 ms). Without a 0 ms or near-0 ms baseline, the authors cannot determine the starting point of the illusion rate and thus cannot fully characterize the temporal trajectory. The 'short' condition may already reflect substantial memory processing.
issues.quote: In two conditions the memory probe appeared 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display, in the third memory condition, the probe appeared 3 seconds after offset of the memory display.

issues.subcategory: Confounded interference and delay conditions
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the 'Short with Interference' condition conflates two manipulations: the interfering visual display appears simultaneously with the cue, meaning participants must process the cue while being exposed to interference. This makes it impossible to separate the effects of visual interference per se from attentional competition at the time of cue processing. The 'Long' condition has neither interference at cue time nor a simultaneous interfering display, making the three conditions non-orthogonal in their manipulation of memory decay mechanisms.
issues.quote: The Short with Interference condition (panel B) was the same as the Short condition, except that now the second letter display appeared together with the cue.

issues.subcategory: Unbalanced trial proportions creating response bias
issues.description: In Experiment 1, real letter targets comprised 75% of trials and pseudo-letter targets 25%. The authors acknowledge this creates a potential response bias but argue the temporal pattern rules it out. However, this imbalance also affects the statistical power for detecting real-to-pseudo illusions (fewer trials) and may inflate pseudo-to-real illusion rates through a simple base-rate effect. Experiments 3 and 4 were designed to address this, but Experiments 1 and 2 remain confounded, and the authors draw conclusions from all four experiments jointly.
issues.quote: The target letter was a real letter in 75% of the trials and a pseudo-letter in the remaining 25%.

issues.subcategory: Large and differential participant exclusion based on confidence rates
issues.description: In Experiment 2, 92 of 290 participants (31.7%) were excluded for having fewer than 10 high-confidence trials in one or more cells. This is a very high exclusion rate. Critically, excluded participants had systematically lower confidence rates (15.7% vs 49.2%), suggesting they may represent a qualitatively different population—perhaps those who were more uncertain or less susceptible to illusions. Excluding them may inflate the observed illusion rates in the retained sample and threatens the generalizability of findings. No sensitivity analysis is reported for the full sample.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions.

issues.subcategory: Exclusion criterion creates circular dependency with dependent variable
issues.description: Participants are excluded based on having too few high-confidence trials, but high confidence is also the dependent variable of interest (illusion rates are computed only on high-confidence trials). This creates a circular dependency: participants who show fewer high-confidence responses—potentially because they are less susceptible to the illusion mechanism—are systematically excluded. This selection bias could artificially inflate the observed illusion rates and the apparent strength of the effect.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory numbers between results sections
issues.description: In the Experiment 1 Discussion, the authors state 'high confidence pseudo-to-real illusions (43%) were almost as prevalent as high confidence selections of the actual pseudo-target (50%)' and 'the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from 29% to 39% and 43%'. However, in the Results section, the reported increase is described as '7% increase from 19% in the short delay to 26% averaged over the short with interference and long delay' for illusory errors. These numbers (19%/26% vs 29%/39%/43%) are inconsistent and appear to refer to different subsets of trials (all targets vs. pseudo-letter targets only), but this is not clearly explained.
issues.quote: the increase in illusory errors (7% increase from 19% in the short delay to 26% averaged over the short with interference and long delay) is larger than other errors (4% increase, from 8 to 12%)... From the Short (memory probe 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display with no visual interference) to the Long condition (memory probe after 3 seconds) or the Short with interference (memory probe after .75 seconds following an interfering display) the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from 29% to 39% and 43%

issues.subcategory: Figure reference error in Experiment 4
issues.description: The Experiment 4 Results section states 'Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials,' but Figure 5 is the figure for Experiment 3. The figure for Experiment 4 is labeled Figure 6. This is a clear internal inconsistency in figure referencing that indicates inadequate proofreading and could confuse readers interpreting the results.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA model comparison showed that the model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, Memory Delay...

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent confidence scale across experiments
issues.description: Experiment 1 used a 2-point confidence scale (1=guess, 2=certain), while Experiments 2, 3, and 4 used a 4-point confidence scale (1-4). The threshold for 'high confidence' is not explicitly defined for the 4-point scale experiments. This inconsistency in measurement makes direct comparison of high-confidence error rates across experiments problematic, yet the authors treat results as directly comparable and pool conclusions across all four experiments.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain)... then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4)

issues.subcategory: High confidence threshold not specified for 4-point scale
issues.description: For Experiments 2, 3, and 4, which used a 4-point confidence scale, the authors never specify what threshold was used to define 'high confidence' trials. It is unclear whether ratings of 3 and 4, or only 4, were classified as high confidence. This omission makes the results impossible to replicate and raises concerns about analytic flexibility in threshold selection.
issues.quote: then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4)

issues.subcategory: Online data collection without experimental control in Experiment 4
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Neurotask, with participants using their own laptops in a Zoom breakout room. This introduces substantial uncontrolled variability in display timing, screen resolution, viewing distance, ambient lighting, and potential distractions. These factors are particularly problematic for a study relying on precise stimulus timing (250 ms memory display, 500 ms vs 3000 ms delays) and visual discrimination of mirrored letters. No validation of timing accuracy or screen calibration is reported.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time. Here, each participant was placed in a Zoom break-out room, and given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.subcategory: Sequential stopping rule with different BF thresholds across experiments
issues.description: Experiment 3 used a stopping rule of BF=6 while Experiment 4 used BF=10 for the same critical test. No justification is provided for why different thresholds were used across experiments. This inconsistency suggests post-hoc adjustment of the stopping criterion, which undermines the validity of the sequential analysis approach and inflates Type I error risk.
issues.quote: once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop... once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration reported
issues.description: None of the four experiments report pre-registration of hypotheses, analysis plans, exclusion criteria, or stopping rules. The sequential Bayesian stopping rules in Experiments 3 and 4 are described post-hoc in the methods without reference to a pre-registered protocol. The choice of which follow-up tests to conduct, which model comparisons to report, and the specific exclusion threshold (10 trials) appear to have been made without pre-specification.
issues.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test

issues.subcategory: Causal claims about world knowledge from correlational design
issues.description: The authors repeatedly claim that 'world knowledge drives STM illusions' and that 'lifelong exposure to the alphabet' causes the asymmetric illusion pattern. However, the design cannot isolate world knowledge from other potential causes such as differential perceptual discriminability of real vs. pseudo-letters, differential encoding strength, or response familiarity effects. No manipulation directly varies world knowledge (e.g., training participants on pseudo-letters to equate familiarity) is included.
issues.quote: The illusory memories are driven by world knowledge: high confidence illusory reports are more likely to involve pseudo-letter to real-letter errors (as real letters are well-studied and much more prevalent in the real world) than the other way around.

issues.subcategory: Alternative explanation of differential perceptual discriminability not ruled out
issues.description: Pseudo-letters are by definition less familiar and may be perceptually less discriminable from their real counterparts than real letters are from pseudo-letters, due to asymmetric perceptual learning effects. The authors attribute the asymmetric illusion rate to world knowledge/priors, but differential perceptual discriminability (real letters being more distinctively represented in the visual system) could produce the same pattern without invoking predictive processing or world knowledge effects on memory per se.
issues.quote: visual similarity between to-be-remembered target and the mirrored counterpart that is presented in the response screen is clearly identical in both cases

issues.subcategory: Operationalization of 'world knowledge' conflates multiple constructs
issues.description: The authors use 'world knowledge' to refer to prior expectations about letter orientation, but this conflates at least three distinct constructs: (1) perceptual familiarity/fluency with real letters, (2) semantic/categorical knowledge that letters have a canonical form, and (3) statistical learning of letter frequency. The experimental design cannot distinguish between these, yet the theoretical interpretation invokes a specific predictive processing account that requires a particular type of prior.
issues.quote: Instead 'world knowledge' (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions.

issues.subcategory: High confidence errors as proxy for 'illusory memories' is not validated
issues.description: The authors equate high-confidence errors with 'illusory memories' (i.e., the participant has a false memory trace). However, high confidence errors could also result from: (1) a response bias toward real letters combined with high confidence in that bias, (2) metacognitive miscalibration, or (3) demand characteristics. No independent validation that high-confidence errors reflect a genuine subjective memory experience (e.g., using remember/know judgments or source monitoring tasks) is provided.
issues.quote: Illusory memories should result in high confidence erroneous responses, where the participants has access to a memory trace (albeit an incorrect memory trace).

issues.subcategory: WEIRD and student sample limitations not acknowledged
issues.description: All experiments used university student samples (predominantly female, age 17-30) from the University of Amsterdam, recruited through a psychology course credit pool. The authors make broad claims about human memory and STM in general without acknowledging that the sample is not representative of the general population. Cultural and educational differences in alphabet familiarity could substantially affect the results, yet no such limitations are discussed.
issues.quote: The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum.

issues.subcategory: Overclaim of generalizability to all STM stages
issues.description: The authors claim their findings apply to 'all stages of STM' including iconic memory, working memory, and fragile memory. However, their shortest delay (500-750 ms) is beyond iconic memory duration, and they explicitly acknowledge they did not test iconic memory. The claim that 'all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories' is therefore not supported by their data.
issues.quote: Our findings suggest that illusory memories can occur during the WM and FM stages of STM... Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM

issues.subcategory: Failure to control for verbal rehearsal
issues.description: Letters are highly verbalizable stimuli, and participants may use verbal rehearsal strategies during the retention interval. Verbal rehearsal could differentially benefit real letters (which have standard phonological representations) over pseudo-letters (which do not). No articulatory suppression task or other control for verbal rehearsal is included. This confound could explain the asymmetric illusion rates without invoking predictive processing or world knowledge effects on visual STM.
issues.quote: FTT does suggest that pseudo-letters have a verbal (the letter itself) and a gist level ('mirrored') representation, while real letters can be stored purely at the verbal level. This would mean that verbal rehearsal is more effective to store a complete representation of real letters in working memory, but not for pseudo-letters.

issues.subcategory: Response display design allows process of elimination
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the response display contained 6 letters: the target, two other letters from the memory display, and 3 new letters. When participants cannot remember the target, they can use process of elimination based on what they remember from the memory display. This strategy could systematically favor selection of the real letter counterpart if participants remember seeing 'a letter at that position' without remembering its orientation. This alternative account is not addressed.
issues.quote: The response display consisted of 6 letters: the target letter (with the same orientation as in the memory display, or mirror reversed), two other randomly selected letters from the memory display, and 3 letters that did not appear in the memory display.

issues.subcategory: Missing accuracy rates for correct responses
issues.description: The paper reports only error rates (illusory and other errors) without reporting overall accuracy rates or correct response rates for each condition. Without knowing the baseline accuracy, it is impossible to evaluate whether the error rates are meaningful relative to overall performance, or to assess whether ceiling or floor effects might be influencing the pattern of results.
issues.quote: For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: Missing effect sizes and descriptive statistics
issues.description: The paper relies exclusively on Bayes Factors for inference and reports only percentage error rates as descriptive statistics. No effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d, eta-squared) are reported for any comparison, making it difficult to assess the practical significance of the effects or to use the data for meta-analyses or power calculations for future studies.
issues.quote: The Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA showed that a model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, and Memory Delay, and a Target Type * Error Type and Memory Delay * Error Type interaction had the best fit (BFm = 18)

issues.subcategory: Appendix model comparisons referenced but not included in manuscript
issues.description: Throughout the results sections, the authors repeatedly reference 'Appendix 1 for full model comparison' for all four experiments. These appendices are not included in the manuscript as provided, making it impossible to evaluate the full model comparison results, assess whether the best-fitting model was selected appropriately, or verify the reported BFm values.
issues.quote: see Appendix 1 for full model comparison and Table 1 for an overview of BFincl for each model component

issues.subcategory: Training exclusion criteria and procedure incompletely reported for Experiments 2-4
issues.description: Experiment 1 describes a detailed training procedure with a 75% accuracy exclusion criterion. Experiments 2, 3, and 4 describe only 12 practice trials with feedback but no equivalent training or performance-based exclusion criterion. It is unclear whether participants in Experiments 2-4 were required to demonstrate any minimum proficiency before the main experiment, creating potential differences in participant quality across experiments.
issues.quote: Before the actual experiment each participant received instructions about the goal of the task... Furthermore, participants performed 12 practice trials.

issues.subcategory: Predictive processing framework not uniquely supported
issues.description: The authors argue their results support a predictive processing account of STM. However, the same pattern of results is equally consistent with simpler accounts such as signal detection theory (pseudo-letters have weaker memory signals, leading to more liberal criterion use favoring real letters), schema-based memory theories, or associative interference. The predictive processing framework is not uniquely tested or falsified by any specific experimental manipulation, making the theoretical interpretation an overclaim.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions

issues.subcategory: Mischaracterization of Fuzzy Trace Theory prediction
issues.description: The authors claim FTT predicts that 'high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories' and then argue this is inconsistent with their data because illusions are abundant despite high similarity. However, FTT's similarity prediction applies to semantic/gist similarity, not perceptual/visual similarity. The mirrored counterpart is visually similar but semantically distinct (pseudo-letter vs. real letter). The authors misapply FTT's predictions to their paradigm.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.subcategory: Lack of awareness check validity
issues.description: In Experiment 2, participants completed a questionnaire about the experiment's purpose, and the authors report that 'the relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.' However, the absence of explicit mention does not confirm that participants were unaware of the contingency—they may have been implicitly aware without being able to articulate it. No formal awareness measure (e.g., forced-choice contingency test) was administered.
issues.quote: Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent BFincl reporting in Table 4
issues.description: In Table 4 (Follow-up ANOVA for non-illusory error rates in Experiment 2), the BFincl for Memory Delay is reported as 0.064, yet the text states 'Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay).' These values are contradictory by several orders of magnitude. Either the table or the text contains a serious error in reporting the Bayes Factor for this effect.
issues.quote: Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)... [Table 4 shows BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay]

issues.subcategory: Set size confound in Experiment 1
issues.description: Experiment 1 used memory displays of either 6 or 8 letters, with different numbers of pseudo-letters depending on set size (1-2 pseudo-letters for set size 6, always 2 for set size 8). The analysis averages across set sizes, but set size is known to affect STM capacity and error rates. The different pseudo-letter proportions across set sizes (16-33% for set size 6 vs. 25% for set size 8) could differentially affect illusion rates. This confound is not analyzed or discussed.
issues.quote: When the memory display consisted of 8 letters, it contained 2 pseudo-letters. When it contained 6 letters, it had a 50% chance of containing 1 pseudo-letter and a 50% chance of containing 2 pseudo-letters.

issues.subcategory: Stimulus size reported in implausibly small units
issues.description: The training stimuli are described as '0.05° × 0.01° in size' for the rectangles. These dimensions (approximately 0.9mm × 0.17mm at 1 meter viewing distance) are implausibly small—far below the resolution of typical displays and below the threshold of visual acuity. This appears to be a reporting error (likely missing a decimal point or wrong units), and the correct stimulus dimensions cannot be determined from the manuscript.
issues.quote: The memory and test displays each consisted of eight white rectangles (0.05◦ × 0.01◦ in size)

issues.subcategory: Viewing distance not reported
issues.description: The manuscript reports stimulus sizes in degrees of visual angle but does not report the viewing distance for any experiment. Without viewing distance, the reported angular sizes cannot be verified or converted to physical dimensions, making replication impossible. This is a basic methodological reporting requirement.
issues.quote: Individual rectangles were evenly distributed on an imaginary circle (radius 4.68◦) around fixation.

issues.subcategory: Feedback during experiment may shape expectations
issues.description: Participants received trial-by-trial feedback ('correct/incorrect') throughout all experiments. In Experiment 2, participants also received block-level performance feedback. This feedback could itself shape participants' expectations about what the correct responses are (i.e., that real letters are more often correct), potentially creating or amplifying the response bias toward real letters that the authors attribute to world knowledge. The effect of feedback on illusion rates is not analyzed.
issues.quote: They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.

issues.subcategory: Null result for cue color interpreted as evidence for specific theoretical claim
issues.description: The failure to find an effect of cue color on illusion rates in Experiment 2 is interpreted as evidence that 'expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.' However, the null result could equally reflect insufficient statistical power for this specific comparison, an ineffective manipulation (participants may not have learned the color-target contingency), or that the manipulation was too subtle. The BF against the effect (BFincl = 0.07) provides evidence for the null but the theoretical interpretation goes beyond what the data support.
issues.quote: This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.

issues.subcategory: Irrelevant second display timing inconsistency across conditions
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the irrelevant second display appears at different times relative to the cue depending on condition: in the Short condition it appears 3.75 seconds after the cue, in the Long condition 1.5 seconds after the cue, and in the Short-with-Interference condition simultaneously with the cue. This means the second display serves different functional roles across conditions (post-response interference vs. concurrent interference vs. pre-response interference), making it impossible to attribute differences between conditions solely to memory delay.
issues.quote: If the memory probe appeared in isolation (the Short and Long conditions), the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset, which meant that the interval between the probe and the irrelevant second display was either presented for 1.5s (Long delay) or 3.75s (short delay).
